meta.title: SpaceX, Landlord to the AI Boom
meta.dek: Four months after the largest IPO in history, renting computers has become SpaceX's biggest business. What does $148 assume about the price of a watt of compute, and what does a Tesla merger do to the answer?
meta.price_note: Oct 20, 2026 close; ≈$161 overnight after the Q3 print
meta.type: Launch, LEO satellite connectivity and AI compute (Super Intelligence) under one roof

verdict.sentence: SpaceX now earns real money, but at $148 the price already pays for my Base case of a compute business that keeps its pricing; the probability-weighted case returns [[pw_return]] a year against the 13% hurdle.
verdict.breaks_if: Compute rental prices fall faster than the GPUs depreciate. Watch the Q1 2027 print against the $33–37B revenue guide, and the funding of a $35–40B capex quarter without selling stock low.
verdict.moat: Wide in launch and Starlink; none yet in compute

call: Q3 settled the first question about SpaceX: the AI build earns money. Super Intelligence revenue rose to $7.6B from $0.8B a year ago, the segment made a profit, and management guided Q1 2027 revenue to $33–37B, roughly a $140B run-rate. The price settled the second question too, in the other direction. At $148, about 75 times run-rate earnings, the stock needs FY2031 EPS near [[Priced-in.eps]] to earn an ordinary 10% a year. That is about 40% of the way from my Base case to my Bull. The Base assumes a 15 GW compute business whose rental price falls to a third of today's scarcity level, and on it the stock earns nothing. So the whole return rests on how long a watt of compute rents for $30–50 a year. Management's answer is that the price per watt is rising and short contracts capture it. Mine is that short contracts cut both ways, and that a $35–40B capex quarter has to be funded at whatever the stock price is. I give the Bear 25%; the price implies [[implied_bear]]. Excellent businesses, a price that leaves no room: [[pw_return]] a year, clearing 13% only at [[entry]].

tests.claim: That compute pricing holds through the build.
tests.test: Q1 2027 revenue (reported late April 2027) inside the $33–37B guide, with Q4 2026 Super Intelligence revenue at or above $12B (late January 2027).
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Bull to Bear (PW EV [[test1.pw_ev]], [[test1.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test1.verb]]**, entry [[test1.entry]].

tests.claim: That the build funds itself without cheap equity.
tests.test: through the Q2 2027 10-Q (early August 2027), no common-stock sale beyond employee pay and announced acquisitions above 2% of shares, the investment-grade rating kept, and cash and securities above $40B.
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Base to Bear (PW EV [[test2.pw_ev]], [[test2.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test2.verb]]**, entry [[test2.entry]]; the reflexive funding loop is live.

tests.claim: That Starship becomes a reusable launch system.
tests.test: both stages caught and a ship reflown by June 30, 2027 (Flight 15 in November is the first catch attempt).
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Bull to Base (PW EV [[test3.pw_ev]], [[test3.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test3.verb]]**, entry [[test3.entry]]; V3 Starlink and Mobile V2 slip a year.

model_build.note: Base case. The first column is the exit run-rate (Q1 2027 revenue guidance of $33–37B annualized, with Q3 2026 segment margins), labelled FY2026E because the model counts five years from it; calendar 2026 revenue will be about $48B. Margins move linearly to the FY2031 inputs. GAAP EPS includes stock pay. Source: author's model (model.json).

scenarios.note: Annual return = price change to the FY2031 value (no dividend). Probabilities apply to Bull, Base and Bear; competence is Outside, so Bull and Bear each get at least 25%. The Priced-in and Hurdle rows are solved along the Base→Bull path at a 30× exit. Option lines are added to the PW value. Source: author's model. Built with Claude.

return_math.compounding: Base run-rate EPS grows [[Base.cagr]] a year to [[Base.eps]], but the multiple falls from about 75× to 30×, so the Base earns about nothing ([[Base.return]] a year). There is no dividend or buyback; net dilution runs 2% a year in the Base. All of the PW return above the Base comes from the Bull's tail, not from compounding at a flat multiple.
return_math.epv: About $20–25 a share: run-rate net income of roughly $25B at 85% owner-earnings conversion, capitalized at 10%, plus $51B of net cash. About 85% of the price pays for growth. The Bear ([[Bear.value]]) sits just above EPV because it keeps Starlink growing while compute stalls.
return_math.base_rate: From a $140B run-rate, the Base grows revenue about 18% a year and the Bull about 38%; fewer than 2% of companies above $50B of sales have grown 20% a year in real terms for five years, so the Bull is possible-to-plausible only because the run-rate itself is brand new. The Base is probable only if the 2027 guide holds; it leans on management's own numbers.
return_math.year_ten: In the Bull, still growing at year ten on compute and Starlink Mobile. In the Base the terminal multiple does most of the work, since compute revenue per GW is assumed to fall.
return_math.terminal_growth: Implied perpetual growth at 10%: Bull [[Bull.g]], Base [[Base.g]], Bear [[Bear.g]], all above the 5.15% Treasury, so every case leans on growth beyond year five. I accept the flag for the Bull and Base, whose stories still grow at year five; the Bear's 22× is generous for a business whose compute stalls.
return_math.note: Computed rows come from model.json; EPV, base rate, year ten and the terminal-growth reading are the author's. Built with Claude.
